pairs.difference: A: the sneaker toe has a crisp, even grid of mesh dots, the laces have sharp colored aglets, and the upper and sole share one satin vinyl sheen. Detail and gloss sit at the top of the real range. This is the over-specified micro detail seen in the generated lesson gloves. B: the candle wax is soft and creamy with quiet highlights on the drips, and the wood grain under it is fine. It is smoother than the real range, but that suits wax.
pairs.fix: Keep the shoe soft and simple: suggest the mesh with a faint tonal patch instead of individual holes, make the upper matte fabric, and keep a soft sheen only on the rubber sole.

pairs.difference: B: the gold frame scrolls are covered in dense, crunchy, sharpened highlight marks, so every curl is equally bright, and the diagonal mirror streaks are decorative. A: the glass, ice and straw are soft and clean, the rim is quiet, and only a few small bubbles carry detail. It measures low on detail, but the surfaces read correctly as glass and liquid.
pairs.fix: Paint the gold frame as smooth cast metal with broad soft reflections and a few small highlights. Remove the fine scratchy marks and leave the recesses matte and darker.

pairs.difference: A: the keys have razor-crisp digits and bevels, and the body has a fine even grain. Detail, micro texture and gloss all exceed the real range, and every key has the same satin lacquer. B: the feeder's boards have quiet painted grain and soft plank edges, and the rope twist is small. It stays within range, though the wood looks somewhat painted.
pairs.fix: Soften the key edges and printed digits slightly, remove the speckled grain from the casing, make the body matte plastic, and keep the shine only on the keys.

pairs.difference: A: the moon crater floors and rim are filled with sharp stippled noise, with scattered tiny pits and a hard bright rim on every crater. Highlight share is 0.308, above the real range, and gloss is almost none, so it reads as one dry plaster. B: the bugle brass has broad smooth reflections, and the rope twist is fine and soft. Brass and cord read as different materials, though the gloss is slightly above range.
pairs.fix: Make the moon surface smooth soft stone with gentle tonal blotches, fewer and softer craters, and no stipple or speckle inside them.

pairs.difference: A: the cabin has quiet door grain and log-end rings with soft-edged shingles, and everything shares a similar satin finish. B: the tiki bar has a speckled concrete counter, glossy fruit and busy thatch. Both are within every measured range, and neither finish clearly departs from the real cards.

B: the iron bars and spear tips have hard, oversharpened edges and an even matte black, and the stone posts carry thin hairline cracks. Micro texture is the higher of the pair. A: the speckled counter is quieter and the stool tops have soft satin highlights. The numbers sit in range for both, so this is a weak lean from edge finish only.
pairs.fix: Soften the edges of the iron bars, add a broad soft sheen along each bar, and remove the hairline cracks from the stone posts.

pairs.difference: A: the locker body, door, vents and feet are all the same thick glossy orange, so painted sheet metal reads as molded plastic, with rounded chunky vent slots. Only the rail reads as metal. B: the armchair velvet has a soft fine nap with a sheen falling off at the folds, distinct from the small brass tacks and satin wood legs.
pairs.fix: Make the locker painted sheet metal: thin flat panels with crisp pressed vents, a matte paint finish with slight wear at the edges, and small metal hinges and rivets.

pairs.difference: B: the map paper is thick glossy white plastic with rounded bevels, and the red X is a shiny toy piece. It has no paper fiber or matte printed look, and highlight share is 0.207, above the real range. A: the lamp has brass with soft broad reflections against frosted, translucent-looking glass, giving two distinct materials and a controlled gloss range.
pairs.fix: Draw the map as thin matte paper with sharp folded creases and slightly worn edges. Print the X and path flat on the paper in ink, with no bevel or shine.

pairs.difference: B: the pillow is one blurred blue mass with a faint weave noise, smeared radial creases and a soft edge. Its seam is barely resolved, and gloss and micro texture are below the real range. A: the lantern has a satin brushed roof, a glass pane with clean edge reflections and a clear matte-to-gloss range, all in range.
pairs.fix: Show a soft fabric pillow with a clear thin stitched seam, gentle puckers beside it and crisp outer edges. Remove the noisy blur from the surface.

pairs.difference: A: the candy is blurred and has no real specular sheen (gloss 0.0, well below the real range), and detail is far below range. Faint repeated diamond marks ghost across the orange and yellow bands like a pattern artifact, not sugar. B: the fruit is busy and sharp, with droplets and seeds, but it is in range, and the glass plate and wet flesh read as different surfaces.
pairs.fix: Draw the candy with a clean smooth waxy sugar surface and one soft sheen along the side. Remove the small diamond marks and keep the color bands sharply in focus.

pairs.difference: A: the rim of the binoculars has streaky brushed lines and the barrel ridges are sharp, on a floor with large decorative plank stripes. It carries noticeably more surface marking than the quiet real cards. B: the horse's wood grain is fine and follows the form, and the red saddle has a soft leather sheen, though the whole toy is evenly satin. A is still in range, so this is a weak lean.
pairs.fix: Replace the streaks on the lens rim with one soft smooth metal highlight, make the green barrels matte rubber, and calm the floor grain to fine, faint lines.

pairs.difference: A: the spider is smooth, soft satin with glossy eyes, and it reads as uniform vinyl. B: the fan has flat purple pleats with faint noise and simple satin wood sticks. Both have very quiet surfaces like the real cards, and both are in range, so the vector gives no reason to choose.

pattern: Generated cards still give themselves away in two opposite ways. Most often they over-resolve the surface: crisp mesh dots, stippled crater noise, scratchy gold, sharp brushed streaks and hard edges, where real cards stay soft and quiet at small scale. The other tell is material failure: one uniform lacquer turns sheet metal and paper into glossy molded plastic, and low-detail cards turn into blur with ghost marks or noise. Real cards keep detail small and soft, and vary gloss by material within one object.
